4148: Lawfulness of the Section 232 steel tariff action; plaintiffs' facial nondelegation challenge to the statute under which the tariff was imposed was rejected, so the tariff stands.
We agree, and we therefore affirm.
4430: Lawfulness of the presidential Section 201 safeguard tariff on crystalline silicon photovoltaic products, including whether the President could act without an ITC remedy recommendation, whether ITC or report defects invalidate the action, and whether the NAFTA Canada exemption determination was reviewable. Court held the action lawful and not reviewable on these grounds.
We conclude that the President's actions here were lawful and that accordingly, appellants have not established a probability of success on the merits as required for a preliminary injunction.
8748: Lawfulness of Proclamation 9980 under Section 232: the President could extend tariffs to steel derivatives after the statutory 90/15-day deadlines because he was modifying a timely adopted plan of action, following Transpacific.

In sum, § 232's deadlines did not prevent the President from modifying his initial timely adopted plan of action by issuing Proclamation 9980, and that conclusion does not render § 232 unconstitutional under the delegation doctrine.
9207: Lawfulness of agency action under the NFA/GCA: whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(o) bars ATF from declaring an amnesty-and-registration period for Previously Excluded Devices (statutory interpretation of the 'under the authority of' exception)
9705: Lawfulness of Proclamation 10101 under the Section 201 safeguard statute: whether the President's interpretation of 19 U.S.C. 2254(b)(1)(B) as permitting trade-restrictive modifications was a clear misconstruction of the statute.
we conclude that the President's interpretation of the applicable statute, which allows him to modify an existing safeguard, is not a clear misconstruction.
9706: Procedural challenge that the domestic industry petition was inadequate to meet the 'on such basis' requirement of 19 U.S.C. 2254(b)(1)(B); court held the government's reading was not a clear misconstruction.
We agree with the trade court that the President did not violate the 'on such basis' procedural requirement for adopting a modification.
9707: Procedural challenge that the President's finding that domestic industry 'has begun to make' a positive adjustment did not satisfy the statutory requirement that industry 'has made' one; court held the distinction not a clear misconstruction.
we hold that the distinction between 'has made' and 'has begun to make' is too narrow to rise to the level of a clear misconstruction.
9708: Procedural challenge that the President had to re-weigh economic and social costs and benefits when modifying a safeguard; court held no such requirement applies to modifications.
We conclude that the President's view that he was not required to re-weigh the costs and benefits when modifying the safeguard pursuant to Section 2254(b)(1) is not a clear misconstruction.
9781: Lawfulness of Proclamation 9772's increase of the Section 232 tariff on Turkish steel under 19 U.S.C. § 1862 (timing of presidential action after the 90- and 15-day periods without a new Secretary report).
We reverse the Trade Court's determination that Proclamation 9772 violated § 1862.
10614: Lawfulness of Section 232 steel tariffs: whether the Secretary's and President's threat determinations and the indefinite-duration tariff violated 19 U.S.C. § 1862 (no imminence requirement; no end date required).
We find no violations of the statute.
11488: Lawfulness of the IEEPA Trafficking Tariffs and Reciprocal Tariffs: the court held IEEPA's regulate-importation authority does not authorize the tariffs, affirming the CIT's holding that they exceed presidential authority.
We affirm the CIT's holding that the Trafficking and Reciprocal Tariffs imposed by the Challenged Executive Orders exceed the authority delegated to the President by IEEPA's text.
13176: Lawfulness of Proclamation 10101: whether 19 U.S.C. § 2254(b)(1)(B) authorizes the President to modify a safeguard in a trade-restrictive direction.
we agree with the government that "modify" here includes trade-restrictive changes.
13177: Procedural prerequisites for presidential modification under § 2254(b)(1)(B): whether a Commission report is required and whether the phrase 'on such basis' refers to it, which the court held the President's action satisfied.

the best reading of Section 2254(b)(1)(B) is that the President's modification power requires (i) a Commission report, (ii) a request from a majority of representatives of the domestic industry, and (iii) a Presidential determination that the domestic industry has made a positive adjustment to import competition.
13178: Whether the President's determination that the domestic industry 'has made a positive adjustment' was permissible when the industry had only begun the adjustment.

we continue to read this provision as sufficiently broad to be satisfied by the President's determination in connection with Proclamation 10101 that the applicable domestic industry "has begun to make" the required positive adjustment.
13179: Whether the President must redo a cost-benefit analysis when modifying a safeguard under § 2254(b)(1); the court held no renewed analysis is required.
the President is not required to re-weigh costs and benefits when modifying a safeguard pursuant to Section 2254(b)(1).
13426: Lawfulness of USTR's Section 301 action: whether Section 307(a)(1)(C) authorized the modified List 3 and List 4A tariffs as 'no longer appropriate' modifications, including the major questions challenge.
We conclude USTR acted properly when it invoked Section 307(a)(1)(C) to promulgate the Lists 3 and 4A tariffs.
14622: Lawfulness of Section 232 tariff action: Commerce's denial of eight steel tariff exclusion requests under Proclamation 9705 and the 2020 Interim Rule, including the timing focus on request date and the record-based weighing of domestic availability.
We see no basis for setting aside Commerce's decisions, and in explaining that conclusion, we largely adopt the Trade Court's persuasive analysis in the CIT 2024 Decision.
